vectors_ruled_out.title: Hook price manipulation — SingleProviderPoolType does not validate hook price bounds
vectors_ruled_out.description: SingleProviderPoolType gets sqrtPriceX96 from ILimitBreakAMMHook.getSqrtPriceX96(). There is no min/max clamp on the returned value. A malicious hook (controlled by an attacker) could return sqrtPriceX96=1 or sqrtPriceX96=type(uint160).max. However, the attacker must be the pool creator to register a custom hook, and must also be the pool's allowed LP to add liquidity. An attacker who controls both the hook and the LP position gains nothing from price manipulation beyond what they already control. No external victim LP exists in SingleProviderPoolType. The hook price gate is enforced at the AMM level (pool creation) and the protocol's design intent is that the hook author IS the LP. Ruled out: no victim, no profit.

vectors_ruled_out.title: Double-truncation in calculateFixedInput/calculateFixedOutput — non-exploitable round-trip deficit
vectors_ruled_out.description: calculateFixedInput uses double mulDiv (round DOWN). calculateFixedOutput uses double mulDivRoundingUp (round UP). At certain sqrtPriceX96 values, the double-truncation in step1 of calculateFixedInput creates a step1 value such that the inverse double-ceiling in calculateFixedOutput cannot fully recover to the original amountIn. Maximum observed deficit: ~200e6 wei (0.0000002 tokens). However, the attacker must pay fees on every swap. Fee at even 1 BPS = 1e14 wei per 1e18 input. The deficit (~2e8) is 6 orders of magnitude smaller than the minimum fee. An iterated extraction loop (swapByOutput to get discounted amountIn, then swapByInput to sell back) results in net LOSS. Confirmed by test_C20_exploit_iteratedExtraction (10 round-trips: net loss of 975e18 token0 due to fee dominance).
vectors_ruled_out.evidence: test_C20_roundTripAlwaysLoses, test_C20_fuzz_multipleAmountsAndPrices, test_C20_exploit_iteratedExtraction in AuditPriceDistorterSP.t.sol. Max deficit bounded at 1e9 wei per round-trip.

vectors_ruled_out.title: First depositor inflation attack (C28 ERC-4626 pattern)
vectors_ruled_out.description: SingleProviderPoolType uses exact-amount deposits, not share-based accounting. addLiquidity returns exact token amounts stored. removeLiquidity checks exact reserve amounts. There are no shares, no share price, no totalSupply to manipulate. The ERC-4626 first-depositor inflation attack is structurally inapplicable.
vectors_ruled_out.evidence: SingleProviderHelper.sol — addLiquidity and removeLiquidity use amount0/amount1 directly with no share math

vectors_ruled_out.title: Cetus-pattern overflow in computeRatioX96 (C26)
vectors_ruled_out.description: SqrtPriceCalculator.computeRatioX96 computes sqrt(price) * 2^96 from raw token price ratios. Overflow to near-zero price would enable extracting massive output for near-zero input. Forge tests with sqrtPriceX96=1 (near-zero price) show the math correctly produces near-zero output amounts — the pool is drained of token0 for near-zero token1 input, but only when the hook itself returns near-zero price. No overflow path exists in the library that produces a near-zero result from a legitimate input. The Cetus bug required a specific tick_index overflow path that does not exist here.
vectors_ruled_out.evidence: test_C26_nearZeroSqrtPriceDrainsPool in AuditPriceDistorterSP.t.sol — confirmed hook must return the bad price, not computable from user input

vectors_ruled_out.title: Unit mismatch in price feeds — D6 token as D18 (C30, C31)
vectors_ruled_out.description: No hidden scaling in SingleProviderHelper. computeRatioX96 accepts raw sqrt price values. All internal math uses Q96 consistently. Cross-contract dimension trace: AMMModule → swapByInput/swapByOutput → calculateFixedInput/calculateFixedOutput → mulDiv/mulDivRoundingUp. Amounts are passed as raw uint256 throughout with no D6/D18 conversion. A 6-decimal token would naturally produce different amounts (1e6 USDC ≠ 1e18 WETH) but the AMM doesn't assume decimals. No unit mismatch vulnerability found.

vectors_ruled_out.title: BPS denominator scaling error — fee-on-gross vs fee-on-net (C34, C39)
vectors_ruled_out.description: Input path fee uses MAX_BPS (10000) denominator: mulDivRoundingUp(amountIn, feeBPS, MAX_BPS). Output path fee uses gross-up denominator (MAX_BPS - feeBPS): mulDivRoundingUp(reserveAmountIn, feeBPS, MAX_BPS - feeBPS). Both formulas are mathematically correct and protocol-favorable. At max fee (10000 BPS), amountOut=0 (100% fee). No fee bypass, no undercollection. Division-before-multiplication patterns absent — all fee math uses mulDivRoundingUp with correct operand order.

vectors_ruled_out.title: Fee path divergence — two fee paths produce different outputs from same input (C17)
vectors_ruled_out.description: Input path (swapByInput): fee = mulDivRoundingUp(amountIn, feeBPS, MAX_BPS) first, then price conversion on net. Output path (swapByOutput): price conversion first, then gross-up fee on reserveAmountIn. These are mathematically different operations. Tested with fee=30 BPS, amount=5_000_000 ether: both paths produce the same amountOut when swapping equivalent token amounts. The fee path divergence is intentional design (input vs output specified swap) and does not create an exploitable arbitrage — both paths charge fees that are protocol-favorable.
vectors_ruled_out.evidence: test_H_R5_CP_02_feePathDivergence in AuditPriceDistorterSP.t.sol — both fee paths produce equivalent results with no exploitable divergence

vectors_ruled_out.title: Silent Q96 truncation at near-max sqrtPriceX96 (C38)
vectors_ruled_out.description: At sqrtPriceX96 near type(uint160).max (≈1.46e48), intermediate products in calculateFixedInput and calculateFixedOutput would require up to 512-bit precision. FullMath.mulDiv handles this via uint256 phantom overflow algebra (512-bit intermediate). Tests confirm no silent truncation at extreme prices — operations either produce correct results or revert on overflow guard. No exploitable precision loss found.

summary: SingleProviderPoolType math is well-hardened. All 8 price distortion hypotheses ruled out. Three key findings: (1) No profitable price manipulation possible without controlling both hook and LP position simultaneously. (2) Double-truncation in calculateFixedInput/calculateFixedOutput creates a bounded non-exploitable deficit (~2e8 wei max), dominated by even 1 BPS fees. (3) All rounding is protocol-favorable — no dust-loop drain possible. Invariants INV-SW02 and INV-SW03 hold. C-MATH checklist 19/20 items covered (C32 and C35 N/A for SingleProviderPoolType). No submittable findings.
profit_question_answer: NO — an attacker cannot make the protocol believe inventory is worth more or less than it really is for one transaction. The hook price is controlled by the pool creator (who is also the LP), and the math contains no overflow path, unit mismatch, or rounding direction error that could be exploited by a third party.
